###### Abstract

Self-evolving reasoning models learn from their own generated questions,
yet repeated self-training can lead to performance collapse. In this
paper, we investigate why performance deteriorates over successive
rounds and how to sustain self-evolution. Our analysis identifies two
recurring quality problems in self-generated questions: invalid
questions and repeated variants of the same mathematical questions.
First, invalid questions become more prevalent across rounds, and
answer-consistency filtering further increases their proportion in
training data. Second, existing question diversity controls based on
lexical similarity can miss mathematically equivalent questions
expressed in different ways, which leads to question diversity collapse
in later training rounds. Building on these findings, we introduce
R-Quest, which uses question validity and novelty feedback to guide
self-evolution. We first train the solver to recognize and reject
invalid questions, then use its judgments to guide questioner rewards
and filter solver training data. To avoid question repetition, we use a
frozen base model to compare sampled question pairs and provide novelty
feedback. Empirically, our method consistently achieves the highest
average performance on 12 benchmarks in mathematical reasoning,
general-domain reasoning, and code generation across two model families.
Additionally, R-Quest maintains stable performance gains over ten rounds
of self-evolution, peaking in the final round and outperforming R-Zero
by 17.32 points.

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](2610.04299v1/rquest_teaser_illustrated.png)

Figure 1: Average performance on seven math benchmarks. R-Quest exceeds
the peak of R-Zero in every round and peaks at round ten, leading by
17.32 points.

Self-evolving reasoning models learn by generating and solving their own
training tasks ([Huang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib32); [Huang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib36); [Tao et al., 2024](#bib.bib33); [Tan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib34); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib35); [Xiang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib41)), reducing their dependence on human-curated data.
Recent frameworks organize this process around questioner and solver
roles: the questioner learns to propose challenging problems, while the
solver learns to solve them, allowing both roles to co-evolve through
reinforcement learning ([Zhao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib23); [Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib24); [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Shi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib37)). However, continued self-evolution can reverse early
gains and ultimately lead to performance collapse ([Huang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1); [Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib7)). In this paper, we
study the practical bottlenecks to sustained self-evolution: _Why does
performance deteriorate over successive rounds, and how can we address
these bottlenecks to achieve sustained self-improvement?_

To understand why these gains fail to persist, we examine the
self-generated questions by R-Zero ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)).
Our analysis reveals two recurring quality issues: (1) invalid questions
and (2) repeated variants of the same mathematical tasks. First, some
generated questions are invalid (e.g., due to ambiguous definitions,
missing conditions or contradictory assumptions), yet the solver is not
explicitly trained to reject such questions, as shown in
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")(a).
The loop therefore lacks a mechanism to exclude or suppress invalid
questions. We find that invalid questions become more prevalent across
rounds and that answer-consistency filtering further increases their
proportion in training data. Our comparison study further shows that
repairing those invalid questions improves solver performance under
matched training settings, indicating that invalid questions are a
contributing factor to performance degradation and motivating explicit
validity feedback during self-evolution.

![Refer to caption](2610.04299v1/148enlarged-export-fixed.png)

Figure 2: Two question-quality problems in self-evolution and how
R-Quest addresses them: (a) R-Quest can recognize and reject invalid
questions; (b) R-Quest can detect repeated mathematical tasks despite
differences in expression.

Second, as shown in
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")(b),
the questioner can repeatedly generate variants of the same underlying
mathematical task by changing the wording, notation, or numerical
parameters, and easily bypass existing repetition penalties. We observe
substantial concentration in a few mathematical task types in R-Zero’s
fifth round training data. Existing diversity controls could split
questions with the same task structure into separate clusters. Because
repetition penalties depend on cluster size, this fragmentation can
weaken the penalty on frequently repeated tasks. These findings suggest
that effective diversity control must be grounded in an understanding of
what a question asks and how it is solved, so that different expressions
of the same task are recognized as repeated training content.

Building on these insights, we introduce R-Quest, which promotes
sustained self-evolution by explicitly assessing the validity of
generated questions and the novelty of their underlying mathematical
tasks. We first train the solver to recognize and reject invalid
questions. During self-evolution, we incorporate its validity judgments
into the questioner’s rewards to discourage invalid generation. We also
assess task novelty through sampled pairwise comparisons, using the
model’s understanding of the questions to identify repeated mathematical
task structures. Together, these judgments restrict the questioner’s
difficulty rewards to questions assessed as valid and novel. Both
feedback signals are generated during subsequent self-evolution without
further calls to stronger external models.

Across two model families, R-Quest achieves the highest domain-average
scores among evaluated methods on 12 benchmarks spanning mathematics,
code generation, and general reasoning. As shown in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
R-Quest sustains its gains over ten rounds of self-evolution, reaching
its best mathematical performance in the final round and outperforming
R-Zero by 17.32 points at the same iteration on Qwen3-4B-Base. After ten
rounds of self-evolution, R-Quest is 5.75 points above the base model,
whereas R-Zero is 11.57 points below it. These results demonstrate that
assessing the validity and task novelty of self-generated questions
provides a practical route to sustained self-improvement.

## 2 Preliminary Study

### 2.1 Background: The Questioner–Solver Framework

Self-evolution for mathematical reasoning commonly adopts a
questioner–solver co-training framework. Following the R-Zero
paradigm ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)), both models share the same
initialization and are trained alternately using Group Relative Policy
Optimization (GRPO) ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)). For each question
$`q`$ generated by the questioner, the frozen solver samples $`M`$
responses. Let $`\tilde{a}(q)`$ be the majority answer and $`a_{j}`$ the
extracted answer of the $`j`$-th response; the solver’s consistency is
defined as
$`s(q)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathbbm{1}[a_{j}=\tilde{a}(q)]`$. The
questioner is trained to generate novel and moderately challenging
questions by rewarding uncertainty, with the reward maximized at
$`s(q)=1/2`$, while penalizing repetition. Questions are grouped by
lexical similarity using pairwise BLEU distances, and each receives a
repetition penalty of $`|C(q)|/B`$, where $`C(q)`$ is its cluster and
$`B`$ is the batch size. Subsequently, the frozen questioner proposes
new questions, and only those satisfying intermediate consistency
($`|{}s(q)-1/2|{}\leq\delta`$) are retained to train the solver. The
solver is then updated via GRPO using self-consistency pseudo-labels,
assigning binary rewards $`\mathbbm{1}[a(y)=\tilde{a}(q)]`$ to its
responses.

### 2.2 Questioning the Questions: Diagnosing Failures in Self-Evolution

(a)

(b)

Figure 3: Question validity rate and solver performance on
Qwen3-4B-Base. (a) Valid-question rates before and after R-Zero’s
answer-consistency filter. (b) Average math reasoning performance of the
solver trained on matched original and repaired datasets.

#### 2.2.1 Invalid Questions in Solver Training

Self-generated questions are not always well posed. Our investigation
into the collapse of R-Zero ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) reveals a
growing proportion of invalid generated questions. We randomly sample
200 questions from the question pool of each of the five R-Zero rounds
and use GPT-5.6-Sol to assess their validity.
Figure [3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2.2 Questioning the Questions: Diagnosing Failures in Self-Evolution ‣ 2 Preliminary Study ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")(a)
shows that the valid-question rate falls from 76.5% in round one to
39.5% in round five, leaving most questions invalid. In addition, R-Zero
would filter questions based on majority-voted answer agreement
$`s(q)`$, retaining those between 0.3 and 0.8. We find that among the
retained questions, the valid question rate is further reduced, reaching
27.64% in round five. Thus, answer-consistency filtering increases the
proportion of invalid questions in solver training data.

Figure 4: Repeated question distribution and BLEU fragmentation in the
fifth round of R-Zero. BLEU separates the illustrated mathematically
equivalent questions into multiple different clusters.

To test whether invalid questions contribute to solver degradation, we
compare GRPO training on matched original and repaired datasets using
Qwen3-4B-Base. Each dataset contains 1,273 questions, including the same
766 valid questions. The remaining 507 questions are invalid in the
original dataset and replaced by their repaired counterparts in the
other. We use GPT-5.6-Sol to repair invalid questions while preserving
the domain and minimizing changes in difficulty.
Figure [3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2.2 Questioning the Questions: Diagnosing Failures in Self-Evolution ‣ 2 Preliminary Study ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")(b)
shows comparable early performance followed by diverging trajectories:
training on the repaired dataset yields a final average score of 49.91
across seven mathematical benchmarks, compared with 46.54 on the
original dataset. These results indicate that invalid training questions
are a contributing factor to solver degradation in self-evolution.

#### 2.2.2 Repetition in Generated Questions

Generated questions can repeat the same mathematical task structure
despite differences in wording, notation, or numerical parameters.
Although R-Zero discourages repetition through BLEU-based clustering,
lexical similarity may not capture repetition at the level of question
types. In
Figure [4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 2.2.1 Invalid Questions in Solver Training ‣ 2.2 Questioning the Questions: Diagnosing Failures in Self-Evolution ‣ 2 Preliminary Study ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
we show a pair of mathematically equivalent questions in two separate
BLEU clusters: they share the same sequence construction and requested
computation, despite differences in wording and indexing.

To quantify the prevalence of repeated question types, we use
GPT-5.6-Sol to group 200 questions randomly sampled from the filtered
question pool generated in R-Zero’s fifth round. Questions in each group
share the same mathematical task structure, and thus should be
considered as “repeated” questions. The grouping protocol is detailed in
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Exercise-Pattern Concentration Analysis ‣ Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").
As shown in
Figure [4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 2.2.1 Invalid Questions in Solver Training ‣ 2.2 Questioning the Questions: Diagnosing Failures in Self-Evolution ‣ 2 Preliminary Study ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
the three largest question types account for 59.5% of the sample. Under
the BLEU-based clustering procedure of R-Zero, the largest type of
question is split into 22 clusters. Such fragmentation can weaken the
repetition penalty (which is based on cluster size) on a frequently
repeated type. These findings motivate us to assess repetition based on
the underlying task structure.

## 3 Method

As shown in
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
R-Quest introduces two forms of feedback to support sustained
self-evolution: (1) validity feedback from a solver initialized to
recognize and reject invalid questions; and (2) novelty feedback from
the frozen base model, which compares sampled question pairs to identify
repeated tasks. These signals guide questioner rewards during
alternating questioner–solver updates.

### 3.1 Validity-Aware Solver Initialization

Our preliminary analysis in
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Questioning the Questions: Diagnosing Failures in Self-Evolution ‣ 2 Preliminary Study ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
examines invalid questions as a contributor to performance collapse
during self-evolution. We thus introduce validity-aware solver
initialization to teach the solver to recognize invalid questions before
self-evolution.

We construct a dataset by deduplicating questions from the solver
training sets of five R-Zero iterations and randomly sampling an equal
number from each iteration. We use GPT-5.6-Sol to annotate these
questions in two stages. First, the annotator attempts to solve each
question and assesses whether it is valid. Second, it independently
solves only the valid questions to produce reference answers. We further
review these answers and discard examples whose answers cannot be
reliably verified. The dataset statistics and annotation protocol are
provided in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Dataset Construction ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
and
[A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Annotation and Answer Review ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
respectively.

We then train the base model with GRPO to return a mathematical answer
for a valid question or INVALID for an invalid one. The model is
instructed to attempt a solution and use INVALID only when it identifies
a flaw in the question itself. We use the reward

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
R_{\text{init}}(q,a)=\mathbbm{1}\!\left[a=a^{*}(q)\right]-\lambda\,\mathbbm{1}\!\left[a=\mathtt{INVALID}\land a^{*}(q)\neq\mathtt{INVALID}\right],
``` |  |

where $`a^{*}(q)`$ is the reference answer for a valid question and
$`\mathtt{INVALID}`$ otherwise, and $`\lambda>0`$ controls the penalty
for rejecting valid questions to discourage excessive refusal. The full
reward specification and training settings are provided in
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Reward and Training Settings ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").
We initialize the solver with this model, bringing its ability to
recognize invalid questions into the self-evolution loop.

### 3.2 Question Novelty Assessment via Sampled Pairwise Judgments

As discussed in
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Questioning the Questions: Diagnosing Failures in Self-Evolution ‣ 2 Preliminary Study ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
question diversity is another dimension along which self-evolution can
collapse. We use the frozen base model to perform diversity judgment
throughout self-evolution. Two questions are considered the same type
when they share essentially the same mathematical setup and ask for the
same kind of task. Changes in numerical values or wording alone do not
establish a new type, while belonging to the same broad mathematical
field is insufficient to establish repetition. The full task
specification is provided in
Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Task Specification ‣ Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").

Let $`B`$ denote the number of candidate questions in a questioner
rollout batch during GRPO training, and let $`p_{ij}\in\{0,1\}`$
indicate whether questions $`i`$ and $`j`$ are judged to be of the same
type. These binary pairwise judgments define an exhaustive novelty gate,
$`\prod_{j\neq i}(1-p_{ij})`$, which equals one only when no repetition
is detected: a single same-type match is sufficient for rejection.
However, evaluating this gate for all candidates requires $`O(B^{2})`$
model judgments.

To reduce this cost, we uniformly sample $`K`$ other questions per
candidate without replacement and reject the candidate if any reference
is judged to be of the same type. This reduces the total comparison cost
to $`O(BK)`$ and relaxes the exhaustive gate, with $`K`$ controlling how
strongly repeated task types are suppressed. Let $`p`$ denote the
fraction of the remaining questions that the judge would classify as the
same type. When $`K`$ is small relative to $`B`$, the probability of
passing is $`\Pr(\mathrm{pass}\mid p)\approx(1-p)^{K}`$. For example,
with $`K=8`$, a same-type fraction of $`10\%`$ yields a pass probability
of approximately $`43\%`$, compared with only $`6\%`$ at a fraction of
$`30\%`$.
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Effect of Random Sampling ‣ Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
provides the exact pass probability and a plot showing how it varies
with the same-type fraction $`p`$ and the comparison budget $`K`$.

### 3.3 Self-Evolution with Validity and Novelty Feedback

##### Questioner Rewards.

We initialize the solver with the validity-aware model from
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Validity-Aware Solver Initialization ‣ 3 Method ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
bringing its ability to recognize and reject invalid questions into
self-evolution. For a generated question $`q`$, it is first instructed
to assess validity while attempting a solution and return INVALID if it
identifies a flaw in the question. We sample multiple responses and
denote the fraction returning INVALID by $`u(q)`$. We define the
validity gate as $`g^{\mathrm{valid}}(q)=\frac{1}{2}-u(q)`$. A question
is classified as invalid when $`g^{\mathrm{valid}}(q)<0`$, meaning that
more than half of the responses return INVALID.

For questions that pass this check, we switch to a standard
problem-solving instruction that asks for reasoning and a final
mathematical answer, and sample a fresh set of responses. Let $`s(q)`$
be the proportion of responses in the largest answer cluster. We define
$`g^{\mathrm{novel}}(q)`$ to be $`1`$ if $`q`$ passes the sampled
novelty check in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Question Novelty Assessment via Sampled Pairwise Judgments ‣ 3 Method ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
and $`0`$ otherwise. The questioner reward is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{\text{question}}(q)=\begin{cases}g^{\mathrm{valid}}(q),&g^{\mathrm{valid}}(q)<0,\\
g^{\mathrm{novel}}(q)R_{\mathrm{uncertainty}}(q),&g^{\mathrm{valid}}(q)\geq 0,\end{cases}\;R_{\mathrm{uncertainty}}(q)=\min\{s(q),1-s(q)\}.
``` |  |

where $`R_{\mathrm{uncertainty}}(q)`$ is the uncertainty reward based on
answer consistency. The questioner is updated with GRPO using this
reward. The prompts for validity assessment and standard problem solving
are provided in the Appendix
Prompts [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Reward and Training Settings ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
and [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Task Specifications ‣ Appendix C Self-Evolution Settings ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
respectively.

##### Solver Updates.

The updated questioner generates candidate training questions. We first
apply the same majority-vote validity check, then sample mathematical
solutions for questions that pass. Consistent with R-Zero ([Huang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib1)), we construct the training set using
answer-consistency filtering and majority-vote pseudo-labels. The solver
is updated with GRPO on this dataset, mixed with a small, fixed
proportion of the solver initialization data to maintain its ability to
recognize and reject invalid questions. Replay examples retain the
validity-aware task and reward defined in
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Reward and Training Settings ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").
The questioner and solver are then updated alternately. Sampling
settings, filtering thresholds, and the replay proportion are provided
in
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Sampling and Training Settings ‣ Appendix C Self-Evolution Settings ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

##### Models and Baselines.

We evaluate Qwen3-4B-Base ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)) and
OctoThinker-3B-Hybrid-Base ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)), covering
Qwen ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)) and Llama ([Grattafiori et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5)) model families. OctoThinker uses mid-training to
address the limited gains from applying GRPO directly to Llama base
models ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)). We compare against the base
models, R-Zero, and two recent methods for stabilizing self-evolution,
OCNR ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)) and R-Diverse ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib7)). Baseline descriptions and implementation details are
provided in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Baseline Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").

##### Evaluation.

We evaluate on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks, three
general-domain reasoning benchmarks, and two code generation benchmarks.
In line with baselines ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Lee et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6)), we report mean@32 on AMC and both AIME benchmarks,
and greedy-decoding accuracy on the remaining reasoning benchmarks. Code
generation is evaluated on HumanEval+ ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib11))
and MBPP+ ([Austin et al., 2021](#bib.bib12)) using EvalPlus ([Liu et
al., 2023](#bib.bib10)), with pass@1 as the metric. For each domain, we
report the checkpoint with the highest average benchmark score across
evaluated rounds. Benchmark descriptions and evaluation settings are
provided in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Benchmarks ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").

##### Training Settings.

All evaluated methods alternate GRPO updates of the questioner and
solver, using a per-round budget of 10,000 candidate questions, with
OCNR requiring twofold oversampling by design. The solver uses the
validity-aware initialization in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Validity-Aware Solver Initialization ‣ 3 Method ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
with 10% replay from the initialization dataset each round. The validity
gate uses majority voting over nine responses, while the novelty gate
uses $`K=8`$ within-batch comparisons judged by a frozen copy of the
corresponding base model. Further training details are provided in
Appendices [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Reward and Training Settings ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
and [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Sampling and Training Settings ‣ Appendix C Self-Evolution Settings ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").

### 4.2 Main Results

Figure 5: Average performance on seven benchmarks over ten rounds on
Qwen3-4B-Base. Yellow and orange denote R-Quest without novelty or
validity feedback.

##### R-Quest outperforms self-evolution baselines in mathematical reasoning.

Consistent with evaluations in previous work ([Huang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1); [Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib7)), we compare all methods
over five rounds of self-evolution, reporting the checkpoint with the
highest mathematical average for each method. As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Training Settings. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
R-Quest achieves the highest average performance across seven
mathematical reasoning benchmarks on both backbones, surpassing R-Zero,
OCNR, and R-Diverse. It improves over Qwen3-4B-Base by 5.47 points and
over OctoThinker-3B by 5.79 points. Relative to R-Zero, R-Quest yields
additional gains of 2.54 and 2.44 points. Across both backbones,
validity-aware initialization yields mathematical performance close to
that of the base models. Most of R-Quest’s gains emerge during
subsequent self-evolution, suggesting that initialization supports later
learning by enabling the solver to provide validity feedback. Measured
from the same base models, R-Quest delivers 1.87 and 1.73 times the
gains achieved by R-Zero, respectively, increasing the benefit of
self-evolution across Qwen and Llama model families.

##### R-Quest sustains gains over extended self-evolution.

We extend self-evolution to ten rounds to assess sustained gains, as
shown in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").
R-Zero peaks at 49.10 in round three, then declines to 34.60 by round
ten, falling below the base model’s score of 46.17. In contrast, R-Quest
retains its gains despite minor fluctuations between rounds: every
checkpoint from rounds one through ten exceeds R-Zero’s best score.
R-Quest ultimately reaches its highest score of 51.92 in round ten,
exceeding R-Zero by 17.32 points at the same iteration. We further find
that either validity or novelty feedback alone achieves a higher peak
score than R-Zero. However, validity feedback is more critical for
sustained gains: its removal leads to late-stage collapse, whereas the
variant without novelty feedback shows a milder decline and remains
above the base model.

##### R-Quest improves code generation and general-domain reasoning.

Prior work has shown that mathematical reasoning training can benefit
performance beyond mathematics ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)). As
shown in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ R-Quest sustains gains over extended self-evolution. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
R-Quest substantially improves code generation across both Qwen and
Llama backbones. Specifically, using a mathematics-focused
self-evolution curriculum, it improves average code generation scores
over the base models by 3.90 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and 5.23 points on
OctoThinker-3B, whereas R-Zero, OCNR, and R-Diverse yield comparatively
modest gains. R-Quest also achieves the highest average performance
across the three general-domain reasoning benchmarks on both backbones.
Validity initialization alone yields only modest gains in both domains;
most of the improvement occurs during subsequent mathematics-focused
self-evolution. Reducing training on invalid questions may limit the
reinforcement of solutions based on unstated assumptions, encouraging
reasoning grounded in the information provided across domains. This is
particularly relevant to code generation, where correct implementations
must satisfy the constraints in the task.

### 4.3 Analysis

#### 4.3.1 Component Ablations

##### Validity and novelty feedback both improve performance.

As shown in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ R-Quest sustains gains over extended self-evolution. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
removing either validity or novelty feedback lowers performance across
all three domains. We also compare with a frozen validity judge setting,
with novelty feedback enabled. This variant underperforms the full
R-Quest across all three domains, supporting that continuous
validity-training through self-evolution is essential.

#### 4.3.2 Validity Assessment During Self-Evolution

##### Self-evolution strengthens validity assessment in R-Quest.

We evaluate each round’s solver validity assessment on the same 297
questions held out from the training process, as described in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Dataset Construction ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").
Using
Prompt [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Reward and Training Settings ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
each solver is instructed to answer valid questions and reject invalid
ones, with one greedy response generated per question. We report
balanced accuracy as
$`\frac{1}{2}(\mathrm{Recall}_{\mathrm{valid}}+\mathrm{Recall}_{\mathrm{invalid}})`$,
where the two terms are the fractions of valid questions accepted and
invalid questions rejected, respectively. R-Quest’s balanced accuracy
increases from 64.80% after initialization to 72.93% in round ten
(Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Self-evolution strengthens validity assessment in R-Quest. ‣ 4.3.2 Validity Assessment During Self-Evolution ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")(a)).
Since a solver that accepts every question achieves 50% balanced
accuracy without detecting any invalid questions, we additionally report
invalid recall to assess this capability directly.
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Self-evolution strengthens validity assessment in R-Quest. ‣ 4.3.2 Validity Assessment During Self-Evolution ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")(b)
shows that R-Quest achieves an invalid recall of 86.36% in round ten,
whereas recall for R-Zero remains between 10.23% and 26.14% across all
ten rounds. Thus, the validity assessment capability of R-Quest
continues to improve through self-evolution.

Figure 6: Validity assessment, question and answer quality during
self-evolution on Qwen3-4B-Base. Panels (a) and (b) show R-Quest’s
improved validity assessment on held-out questions. Panels (c) and (d)
show that R-Quest maintains high question validity and better preserves
majority-answer accuracy on valid questions. Bands in (c) show pointwise
95% Wilson confidence intervals.

##### R-Quest generates more valid questions.

We next examine whether stronger solver validity assessment is
accompanied by improved question quality. For each method and round, we
randomly sample 200 questions from the unfiltered pool generated by
their questioner. We query GPT-5.6-Sol to assess each question’s
validity and compute the validity rate.
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Self-evolution strengthens validity assessment in R-Quest. ‣ 4.3.2 Validity Assessment During Self-Evolution ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")(c)
shows that R-Quest increases this rate from 88.0% in round one to
94.5–97.5% throughout rounds four to ten. In contrast, the rate for
R-Zero falls from 76.5% to 49.0%. This indicates that R-Quest steers
question generation toward valid problems as self-evolution proceeds.

##### R-Quest solver derives more reliable answers.

Question generation and answer supervision are coupled across rounds:
generated questions shape solver training, and the updated solver
supplies pseudo-labels for subsequent rounds. Among the 200 questions
sampled for each method and round, we evaluate majority-answer accuracy
only on those judged valid, since invalid questions do not provide
well-defined mathematical targets for solver training. We query
GPT-5.6-Sol independently to derive and verify reference answers, and
compare the majority-voted answers with these references. We report
strict accuracy over questions with verified references, giving no
credit to missing answers or unresolved judgments.
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Self-evolution strengthens validity assessment in R-Quest. ‣ 4.3.2 Validity Assessment During Self-Evolution ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")(d)
shows that the two methods begin with comparable accuracy, but by round
ten, R-Quest retains 54.69% accuracy, whereas R-Zero falls to just
2.06%. This shows that the deterioration in R-Zero extends from question
generation to answer supervision. By maintaining a predominantly valid
question distribution and more reliable pseudo-labels, R-Quest preserves
the quality of self-generated supervision that supports sustainable
self-evolution.

#### 4.3.3 Question Diversity During Self-Evolution

##### R-Quest limits the concentration of recurring exercise patterns.

Following the analysis in
Section [2.2.2](#S2.SS2.SSS2 "2.2.2 Repetition in Generated Questions ‣ 2.2 Questioning the Questions: Diagnosing Failures in Self-Evolution ‣ 2 Preliminary Study ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
we uniformly sample 200 solver training question records without
replacement for each method and round over the first five rounds.
GPT-5.6-Sol sequentially groups them by their underlying mathematical
construction and requested task. We measure concentration using the
top-five share, the fraction of questions in the five largest groups,
averaged over three random orderings of the same sample.
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Exercise-Pattern Concentration Analysis ‣ Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
provides the grouping procedure and task specification. As shown in
Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Overly strict diversity control can limit mathematical gains. ‣ 4.3.3 Question Diversity During Self-Evolution ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
the top-five share for R-Zero rises from 17.0% to 69.0% between rounds
one and five. R-Quest with the default $`K=8`$ remains less concentrated
throughout, reaching 24.0% in round five while maintaining higher
performance.

##### Overly strict diversity control can limit mathematical gains.

Figure 7: Question type clusters (bars, left axis) and mathematical
performance (lines, right axis) on Qwen3-4B-Base. Numbers above the bars
denote top-five group proportion.

We further examine the strength of novelty control in
Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Overly strict diversity control can limit mathematical gains. ‣ 4.3.3 Question Diversity During Self-Evolution ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
by increasing $`K`$ from its default value of 8 to 16, with other
settings unchanged. A larger $`K`$ increases the probability that
questions from recurring exercise patterns are rejected by the novelty
gate (Appendix
Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ B.2 Effect of Random Sampling ‣ Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")).
This further lowers the top-five share, most notably from 30.0% to 16.8%
in round four. However, performance remains below that of $`K=8`$
throughout, suggesting that overly strict diversity control may suppress
more challenging variants within recurring exercise patterns. Effective
novelty control should therefore balance exploration of new exercise
patterns with progress toward harder problems within existing ones.

## 5 Related Work

##### Self-improving Reasoning Models.

Label-free reinforcement learning uses model confidence, answer
agreement, and entropy as training signals ([Zhao et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib20); [Zuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib21); [Agarwal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)). Complementary work learns to generate training tasks
through self-play. Absolute Zero validates tasks and solutions through
code execution ([Zhao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib23)), while R-Zero ([Huang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) and Self-Questioning Language Models ([Chen et
al., 2026](#bib.bib24)) train question generators and solvers using
model-derived feedback. Related frameworks ground learning in games,
document corpora, vision tasks, and tool environments ([Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib25); [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Yue et al.,
2026](#bib.bib27); [Huang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib28); [Huang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib38); [Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib40); [He et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39); [Dai et al., 2026](#bib.bib43); [Sun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib44)). Our work examines the conditions under which
self-generated questions support sustained improvement, focusing on
question validity and task novelty.

##### Question Validity and Diversity in Self-evolution.

For validity, prior work studies question validity in synthetic
mathematical data ([Liang et al., 2026](#bib.bib29); [Shen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30); [Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)). For self-evolution,
VHG ([Lai et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)) relies on a stronger external model
(GPT-5.4) to verify general mathematical problems during self-play. We
teach the solver to reject invalid questions through mid-training,
avoiding calls to stronger external models during subsequent
self-evolution. For diversity, recent methods assess novelty using
distances between solver representations or code-embedding
similarity ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib6); [Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib7)). R-Diverse targets repetition in underlying reasoning
procedures, but relies on an additional code generator
(Qwen2.5-Coder-7B ([Hui et al., 2024](#bib.bib9))) and code encoder
(Jina-Code-Embeddings-1.5B ([Kryvosheieva et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)))
during self-evolution. This departs from the goal of self-contained
self-evolution, where the model generates its own training feedback. We
instead reduce novelty assessment to an atomic judgment of whether two
questions are variations of the same mathematical task, allowing a
frozen copy of the same base model to provide novelty feedback with only
a few random within-batch comparisons.

## 6 Conclusion

We identified invalid questions and repeated mathematical tasks as two
bottlenecks to sustained self-evolution. R-Quest addresses these
bottlenecks by enabling the solver to recognize and reject invalid
questions and using validity and task-level novelty feedback to guide
question generation. Across two model families and 12 benchmarks,
R-Quest achieves the highest domain-average scores among evaluated
methods in mathematics, code generation, and general reasoning. It
further sustains gains over ten rounds on Qwen3-4B-Base, reaching its
best mathematical performance in the final round. Further analyses show
that R-Quest strengthens validity assessment, limits task repetition,
and maintains more reliable majority-vote supervision across rounds.
These findings highlight the ability to assess self-generated questions
as a key component of sustained self-improvement.

Generative AI was used in the research workflow for synthetic data
generation, model-based annotation and verification, and evaluation, and
is also integral to the proposed self-evolution method as described in
the paper. It was additionally used for limited language editing.
AI-assisted research outputs were reviewed using the validation and
consistency-checking procedures described in the paper. The authors
reviewed the final manuscript and take responsibility for its contents.

### Reproducibility Statement

We provide the information required to reproduce the main training and
evaluation pipeline in the paper and appendices.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
describes construction of the validity-aware initialization dataset, the
annotation and reference-answer review procedures, the complete prompts,
reward function, and mid-training hyperparameters.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
specifies the semantic novelty judgment and sampling procedure.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Self-Evolution Settings ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
provides the question-generation and problem-solving prompts,
question-evaluation procedure, solver-data construction, replay
strategy, sampling parameters, and GRPO training settings.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Baseline Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
documents the implementations and configurations of the R-Zero, OCNR,
and R-Diverse baselines, and
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Benchmarks ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
specifies the evaluation benchmarks, decoding procedures, answer
judging, and reported metrics.

## Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details

### A.1 Dataset Construction

We collect questions from the solver training sets of the first five
R-Zero ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) rounds using
Qwen3-4B-Base ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)). After deduplication
within and across iterations, we randomly sample 460 questions per
iteration, assigning 400 to training and 60 to validation. Annotation
and answer review yield a final dataset of 2,240 questions, with
statistics reported in
Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.1 Dataset Construction ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").
Table [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ A.1 Dataset Construction ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
reports the distribution of error types among invalid questions.

Table 4: Dataset statistics for validity-aware solver initialization.

| Split      | Valid | Invalid | Total |
|------------|-------|---------|-------|
| Training   | 802   | 1,141   | 1,943 |
| Validation | 121   | 176     | 297   |
| Total      | 923   | 1,317   | 2,240 |

| Error type              | Count | Percentage |
|-------------------------|-------|------------|
| Contradiction           | 380   | 28.9%      |
| No solution             | 362   | 27.5%      |
| Ambiguity               | 315   | 23.9%      |
| Missing information     | 181   | 13.7%      |
| Poorly formed questions | 72    | 5.5%       |
| Other                   | 7     | 0.5%       |
| Total                   | 1,317 | 100%       |

Table 5: Error types among the 1,317 invalid questions in the training
and validation splits.

### A.2 Annotation and Answer Review

We use gpt-5.6-Sol to annotate the questions in two stages. Both stages
use only the question, without the original R-Zero pseudo-label. First,
the model attempts to solve each question and assesses whether it is
valid using
Prompt [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Annotation and Answer Review ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").
Category A is mapped to VALID, and B–F to INVALID.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Second, a separate call independently solves the valid questions to
produce reference answers using
Prompt [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Annotation and Answer Review ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We then review the reference answers and exclude questions whose answers
cannot be reliably verified.
Prompts [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Annotation and Answer Review ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
and [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Annotation and Answer Review ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
provide the review instructions, with the latter used for questions
requiring further review. Questions flagged for HUMAN_REVIEW were
manually reviewed and retained only when their validity and reference
answers could be verified; unresolved cases were excluded.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A.3 Reward and Training Settings

We train Qwen3-4B-Base ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)) and
OctoThinker-3B-Hybrid-Base ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)) with GRPO to
return a mathematical answer for a valid question or INVALID for an
invalid one, using
Prompt [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Reward and Training Settings ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Rewards are computed from the final output in `\boxed{}`. Rejection
means returning INVALID as the final answer. Mathematical correctness is
evaluated against the reviewed reference answer using the mathruler
equivalence grader used in R-Zero. For responses with a non-empty final
answer box, we apply the reward in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Validity-Aware Solver Initialization ‣ 3 Method ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
with $`\lambda=0.5`$:

|     |                                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       r=\begin{cases}1,&\text{correct answer or correct rejection},\\
       -0.5,&\text{rejection of a valid question},\\
       0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
       ```                                                              |     | (1) |

Responses with a missing or empty answer box receive a reward of
$`-0.1`$.

We sample eight responses per question and compute GRPO advantages
within each group, with a KL penalty relative to the base model. The
checkpoint at step 15 initializes the solver for self-evolution.
Table [6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ A.3 Reward and Training Settings ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
summarizes the training settings.

| Setting                     | Value       |
|-----------------------------|-------------|
| Training steps              | 15          |
| Questions per rollout batch | 512         |
| Responses per question      | 8           |
| Actor global batch size     | 128         |
| Learning rate               | $`10^{-6}`$ |
| KL coefficient              | $`10^{-2}`$ |
| Sampling temperature        | 1.0         |
| Top-$`p`$                   | 0.99        |
| Maximum prompt tokens       | 2,048       |
| Maximum response tokens     | 4,096       |

Table 6: Training settings for validity-aware solver initialization.

## Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment

### B.1 Task Specification

The frozen base model compares a candidate question (Question A) with a
sampled reference (Question B) using the task specification in
Prompt [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Task Specification ‣ Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.2 Effect of Random Sampling

Consider a candidate among the $`B`$ successfully parsed questions in a
Questioner rollout batch. Each batch initially contains 2,048 generated
candidates. Among the other $`B-1`$ questions, let $`m`$ be classified
as the same exercise type by the judge, with $`p=m/(B-1)`$. The
candidate passes the novelty check only if none of its $`K`$ references
is classified as the same type. Uniform sampling without replacement
gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P_{\mathrm{pass}}(B,m,K)=\frac{\binom{B-1-m}{K}}{\binom{B-1}{K}},\qquad K\leq B-1,
``` |  | (2) |

where $`\binom{n}{K}=0`$ for $`n<K`$. When $`K`$ is small relative to
$`B`$, the same-type fraction changes little across successive draws,
yielding

|     |                                           |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       P_{\mathrm{pass}}(B,m,K)\approx(1-p)^{K}.
       ```                                        |     | (3) |

Figure 8: Approximate pass probability $`(1-p)^{K}`$ for the default
comparison budget $`K=8`$ and the additional setting $`K=16`$.

Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ B.2 Effect of Random Sampling ‣ Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
compares the default $`K=8`$ with the additional $`K=16`$ setting.
Increasing the comparison budget makes same-type matches more likely,
raising the probability of rejection. For example, when a recurring
exercise pattern accounts for 5% of the other candidates in the batch,
increasing $`K`$ from 8 to 16 lowers the approximate pass probability
from 66.3% to 44.0%. For a more frequent pattern accounting for 20% of
the other candidates, the pass probability drops from 16.8% to just
2.8%.

Thus, $`K=8`$ already provides substantial suppression: candidates from
a pattern with a 20% share are rejected about five sixths of the time.
Increasing $`K`$ to 16 raises this rejection probability to 97.2%,
leaving very few candidates of that type eligible for the uncertainty
reward. This helps interpret the results in
Section [4.3.3](#S4.SS3.SSS3 "4.3.3 Question Diversity During Self-Evolution ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
where $`K=16`$ lowers the top-five share but yields worse mathematical
performance than $`K=8`$. Overly strict novelty control may suppress not
only repeated exercises but also more challenging variants within the
same pattern, limiting opportunities for further learning. The default
budget therefore balances suppression of recurring patterns with room
for continued exploration within them.

### B.3 Exercise-Pattern Concentration Analysis

We analyze the sampled training records without additional filtering or
deduplication. Only question text is supplied to the evaluator; method
names, round indices, solver responses, and group sizes are withheld.
All methods and rounds use the same evaluator and prompt.

For each ordering, grouping starts with an empty inventory. Questions
are processed one at a time using
Prompt [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Exercise-Pattern Concentration Analysis ‣ Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").
Each existing group is represented by a short pattern description and
the question that established it. A question either joins an existing
group or establishes a new group with its own description and
representative. Existing descriptions and representatives remain fixed
throughout the pass. Each question is assigned to exactly one group.

We repeat this procedure from an empty inventory under three random
orderings of the same 200 records. For each pass, we sum the sizes of
the five largest groups and divide by 200, or sum all groups if fewer
than five are formed. We report the mean top-five share across the three
orderings.

## Appendix C Self-Evolution Settings

### C.1 Task Specifications

We use the question-generation and mathematical problem-solving
instructions from R-Zero ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)), provided in
Prompts [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Task Specifications ‣ Appendix C Self-Evolution Settings ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
and [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Task Specifications ‣ Appendix C Self-Evolution Settings ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
respectively. Validity checks use
Prompt [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Reward and Training Settings ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models"),
and semantic comparisons use
Prompt [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Task Specification ‣ Appendix B Semantic Novelty Assessment ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### C.2 Sampling and Training Settings

##### Questioner Rewards.

To evaluate each generated question, the frozen solver first produces
nine validity responses. A question is rejected if more than half of the
outputs are INVALID. For questions that pass, we sample ten fresh
mathematical solutions to compute answer consistency. These signals,
together with the novelty judgment, determine the questioner reward
defined in
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Self-Evolution with Validity and Novelty Feedback ‣ 3 Method ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").
Questions that fail the required output format receive a reward of
$`-1`$.

##### Solver Data Construction.

After updating the questioner, we generate candidate training questions
and apply the same evaluation procedure: nine validity responses,
followed by ten mathematical solutions for questions that pass. We
retain questions with answer consistency $`s(q)\in[0.3,0.8]`$ and a
non-empty majority-vote answer, which serves as the pseudo-label.

##### Solver Training and Replay.

Replay examples are sampled from the training split of the mid-training
dataset to constitute $`10\%`$ of the mixed solver dataset. They retain
the validity-aware task and reward from
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Reward and Training Settings ‣ Appendix A Validity-Aware Mid-Training Details ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models").
On newly generated questions, the solver uses the standard mathematical
problem-solving task and the R-Zero training reward: $`0.9`$ for
agreement with the pseudo-label under mathematical equivalence checking,
plus $`0.1`$ for placing reasoning inside \<think\> and \</think\> tags
followed by a boxed answer.

##### Shared Settings.

For question evaluation and GRPO rollouts, we use a sampling temperature
of 1.0 and a maximum response length of 4,096 tokens. Both the
questioner and solver are trained with a learning rate of $`10^{-6}`$, a
KL coefficient of $`10^{-2}`$, and a maximum prompt length of 2,048
tokens.
Table [8](#A3.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Shared Settings. ‣ C.2 Sampling and Training Settings ‣ Appendix C Self-Evolution Settings ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
reports question evaluation settings, while
Table [8](#A3.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Shared Settings. ‣ C.2 Sampling and Training Settings ‣ Appendix C Self-Evolution Settings ‣ Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models")
reports GRPO training settings. Responses per input in the latter refer
to training rollouts.

|                                      |               |
|--------------------------------------|---------------|
| Setting                              | Value         |
| Validity responses per question      | 9             |
| Math solutions per accepted question | 10            |
| Top-$`p`$                            | 1.0           |
| Top-$`k`$                            | 40            |
| Consistency filter for solver data   | $`[0.3,0.8]`$ |

## Appendix D Baseline Details

##### Base Models.

We evaluate Qwen3-4B-Base ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)) and
OctoThinker-3B ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)) without additional
training to establish their performance before self-evolution.

##### R-Zero.

We use the released implementation of R-Zero ([Huang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)), which alternates reinforcement learning updates of a
questioner and a solver. The questioner reward combines solver
uncertainty with a BLEU-based penalty for within-batch repetition.
Generated questions are assigned pseudo-labels through majority voting
and used for subsequent solver training.

##### OCNR.

We implement OCNR ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)) from its published
description within the R-Zero training framework. OCNR augments the
questioner reward with a novelty score from a one-class detector trained
to distinguish questions used for solver training from questions
withheld from training. Following OCNR’s twofold overgeneration scheme,
we generate 20,000 candidate questions per round, twice our standard
budget. The detector maintains one learnable center in the solver
representation space. Using values reported in the paper, we set the
novelty reward coefficient to $`0.3`$, the distance temperature
$`\tau=0.5`$, and the EMA update weight $`\alpha=0.05`$. Question
representations are obtained by mean-pooling the solver’s final-layer
hidden states. The detector receives one full-batch SGD update per round
with a learning rate of $`7\times 10^{-3}`$.

##### R-Diverse.

We implement R-Diverse ([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib7)) from its
published description within the R-Zero training framework. It penalizes
repetition based on how questions are solved, both within the current
batch and across rounds. Following the published configuration, we use
Qwen2.5-Coder-7B ([Hui et al., 2024](#bib.bib9)) with greedy decoding to
represent questions as solution programs and
Jina-Code-Embeddings-1.5B ([Kryvosheieva et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)) to
measure their similarity within the current batch and against earlier
questions. For within-batch repetition, we retain R-Zero’s
average-linkage clustering with a cosine-distance threshold of $`0.5`$.
Following the paper, we set the coefficients of the within-batch and
cross-iteration repetition penalties to $`1`$. The memory penalty
combines maximum and mean cosine similarities with equal weights and
thresholds of $`0.5`$ and $`0.25`$, respectively. From the second round
onward, historical examples are uniformly sampled to constitute $`30\%`$
of the solver training data.

## Appendix E Evaluation Benchmarks

Although our self-evolution process focuses on mathematical questions,
we evaluate both mathematical reasoning and its generalization to other
domains. Our evaluation covers mathematical reasoning, general-domain
reasoning, and code generation.

##### Mathematical Reasoning.

We evaluate on seven benchmarks: AMC, Minerva ([Lewkowycz et al.,
2022](#bib.bib13)), MATH-500 ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib14)),
GSM8K ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib15)), OlympiadBench ([He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib16)), AIME24, and AIME25. We use Qwen3-32B ([Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3)) to judge the equivalence of model answers and
reference answers. Consistent with R-Zero ([Huang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)), we report mean@32 on AMC and both AIME benchmarks,
and accuracy under greedy decoding on the remaining benchmarks.

##### General Domain Reasoning.

We evaluate generalization beyond mathematics on three benchmarks:

- •
  MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)): Multiple-choice questions
  across 14 academic domains, requiring both subject knowledge and
  reasoning.
- •
  SuperGPQA ([Du et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)): Graduate-level
  multiple-choice questions across 285 disciplines, assessing
  specialized knowledge and reasoning.
- •
  BBEH ([Kazemi et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)): Challenging tasks covering
  logical deduction, spatial reasoning, and multi-step computation.

We follow the R-Zero evaluation protocol and report exact-match accuracy
under greedy decoding.

##### Code Generation.

We evaluate code generation on two Python programming benchmarks:

- •
  HumanEval+ ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib11); [Liu et al.,
  2023](#bib.bib10)): Completing Python functions given their signatures
  and natural-language specifications.
- •
  MBPP+ ([Austin et al., 2021](#bib.bib12); [Liu et al.,
  2023](#bib.bib10)): Generating short Python programs from
  natural-language descriptions of basic programming tasks.

We use greedy decoding and report pass@1 on the full EvalPlus test
suites.
````
